analysis.one_liner: Strips the legal shield that protects ICE agents from being personally sued for violating people's constitutional rights.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would let people sue ICE agents personally for constitutional violations, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and has seen no action since August 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: When someone is harmed by a federal agent, courts usually dismiss the lawsuit under a doctrine called qualified immunity, which protects officials unless they violated a right that was already 'clearly established' by earlier court decisions. This bill would change that for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents specifically: courts could no longer excuse an agent's conduct because the agent acted in good faith or because the right wasn't clearly established. In practice, that would make it much easier for people — including immigrants and U.S. citizens wrongly detained or mistreated — to sue ICE agents personally and win damages. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: People who are harmed by ICE agents — including immigrants and U.S. citizens wrongly detained or subject to mistreatment — would gain a realistic path to sue the individual agent for money damages. Today, qualified immunity usually ends those cases before a jury hears them [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Under current law, a person harmed by an ICE agent usually loses because courts apply qualified immunity, dismissing the case unless a prior court ruling clearly established the right was violated. The bill would write into federal law that neither good faith nor the absence of a 'clearly established' precedent can be a defense for ICE agents [S2].

The change applies to suits under 42 U.S.C. 1983 — the federal civil rights statute — and any other federal law, letting victims seek money damages from the individual agent rather than being limited to suits against the government [S2].

analysis.who_pays: ICE agents would bear personal financial and legal risk for their conduct in the field, losing the good-faith and 'clearly established' defenses that currently shield them [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill removes both of the standard shields — the good-faith defense and the 'clearly established rights' rule — meaning an ICE agent could face personal damages even when acting on a reasonable, good-faith understanding of the law [S2].

Critics of ending qualified immunity argue that personal liability could make agents hesitant to act, or attract opportunistic lawsuits, raising the cost and difficulty of federal immigration enforcement [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it aims to help — immigrants and citizens harmed by ICE conduct — the bill would remove the main legal shield that lets those cases be dismissed before a jury hears them [S2]. The trade-off it accepts is that agents would face personal legal risk for split-second enforcement decisions, with no good-faith escape [S2]. The larger problem is that the bill has no Republican support and has not moved at all since it was referred to the Judiciary Committee, so its benefits are currently theoretical [S1][S4].

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee in August 2025, and nothing has happened to it since.

narrative.text: The bill's only action was referral to the House Judiciary Committee on August 8, 2025 — the same day it was introduced [S4].
No hearings, markup, committee vote, or floor action has followed, and the Congress is still in session, so the bill remains pending rather than dead [S1].
Its only cosponsors are two Democrats, giving it no visible bipartisan support [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody is better off yet: the bill did not move, but no opposing law was enacted either. ICE agents keep their current legal immunity, and people harmed by them keep the same limited ability to sue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; bill sits untouched in committee

for.name: Rep. Shri Thanedar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to end qualified immunity for ICE agents [S1][S2].

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction [S2][S3].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on August 8, 2025 and has taken no action — no hearings, no markup, no vote [S4].

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters — the sponsor and two cosponsors — are Democrats; there is no Republican support in the record [S3].

industries.note: Agents would lose the qualified-immunity defense that currently shields them personally from damages lawsuits, exposing them to individual liability for constitutional violations [S2].
The agency could no longer rely on qualified immunity to get cases dismissed early, increasing litigation costs, though the statute targets individual agents rather than agency budgets [S2].

analysis.trajectory: Bills from minority-party members that sit in committee with no cosponsors beyond one or two almost never advance; unless the bill gains significant support or the committee schedules action, it will likely expire without a vote at the end of the 119th Congress.
